title: Maternal high-fat diet modifies myelin organization, microglial interactions, and results in social memory and sensorimotor gating deficits in adolescent mouse offspring.
ehr_evidence: C57BL/6N female mice aged 5 – 6 weeks were obtained from Charles River and habituated to pair-housing for one week.
summary: Preclinical study investigating how maternal high-fat diet modifies myelin organization, microglial interactions, and behavioral outcomes in adolescent mouse offspring.
key_findings: Increased myelin optical density in mHFD-exposed male offspring compared to female mHFD-exposed offspring (p=0.0082).
Reduced area of cytosolic myelin channels in mHFD-exposed male offspring compared to control males (p=0.0016).
Lower hippocampal expression of Mbp, Cspg4, Olig2, and Igf1 in mHFD-exposed males (Mbp p=0.0014 vs male CD).
mHFD-exposed microglia exhibited reduced numbers of mature tertiary lysosomes and increased synaptic contacts.
mHFD-exposed offspring of both sexes showed decreased social novelty preference and reduced prepulse inhibition at 9 dB prepulse.
No significant differences in oligodendrocyte density, distribution, or maturation between diet groups.
captured_features: cytosolic myelin channel area and ratio
gene expression (Mbp, Cspg4, Olig2, Igf1, Gpnmb)
behavioral metrics (social preference, social novelty preference, anxiety index, prepulse inhibition)
population: adolescent C57BL/6N mouse offspring (male and female)
limitations: preclinical mouse model limits direct human translation
small sample sizes per group (n=4-5 animals)
lack of direct microglial modulation to establish causality
sex-specific mechanisms not fully elucidated beyond male/female dichotomy
